note: Part B (drawing) is not transcribed: no model answer exists.

questions.text: Shown below are sole designs of slippers, of which some are matched-pairs (one left foot and one right foot). Identify the total number of matched-pairs in the image.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: There are 13 soles. A matched pair needs the same design with one sole the mirror image of the other. Seven soles carry the same design and all belong to the same foot, so none of them pairs with another. The remaining six soles form three mirror-image pairs, so there are 3 matched pairs.

questions.text: X1 is a 3D form generated from the shape X, using certain 3D operations. It has 11 surfaces in total. If the same operations are carried out on shape Y, how many surfaces would the resulting 3D form have?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: X1 is shape X extruded and bent into a V, so each of the 5 sides of X gives a face in each arm (10 faces) plus 2 end faces, which would make 12. The count is 11 because the side parallel to the dashed line stays one flat face across the bend. Shape Y has 12 edges (circle arc, 2 neck edges, 4 diamond edges and 5 edges of the hole), 4 of them parallel to the dashed line. So Y gives 2 x 12 + 2 - 4 = 22 surfaces.

questions.text: Fifteen people from different places came together for a family reunion. Each one of them had two gifts each for every other person. When the gifts were exchanged they hugged each other. What is the difference between the number of hugs and the number of gifts exchanged?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Each of the 15 people gives 2 gifts to each of the other 14, so 15 x 14 x 2 = 420 gifts. Each pair of people hugs once when they exchange gifts, and there are 15 x 14 / 2 = 105 pairs. The difference is 420 - 105 = 315.

questions.text: A tetrahedral puzzle is made of smaller tetrahedrons. Shown below is one side of the puzzle and a small tetrahedron. Assuming that all the faces of the puzzle are same, how many small tetrahedrons are there on the faces of the larger tetrahedron?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Each face shows 16 small triangles, each the face of a small tetrahedron, so the four faces show 64 triangles. A corner tetrahedron appears on 3 faces: the 4 corners are counted 12 times but are only 4 pieces, so subtract 8. Each edge has 2 non-corner tetrahedra that appear on 2 faces: 12 pieces counted twice, so subtract 12. That leaves 64 - 8 - 12 = 44.

questions.text: The picture shows decimal numbers encoded in colors in some other number system. Encodings of six numbers have been given in the picture on the left. Picture on the right shows a multiplication that we need to perform. What decimal number represents the result of this multiplication?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The colours are base-3 digits: green = 0, red = 1, blue = 2. Check: 3 = 010 (green red green), 10 = 101, 21 = 210, 23 = 212, 24 = 220. Red green green = 100 in base 3 = 9, and green green blue = 002 = 2. So 9 x 2 = 18.

questions.text: A cube has its six faces numbered 1 to 6. A school boy tosses up the cube twice and notes down the two numbers appearing on top in these two tosses. He multiplies these two numbers and notes down the multiplication result. How many unique multiplication results can he possibly get through this tossing game?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: List the products of two numbers from 1 to 6: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20, 24, 25, 30, 36. Repeats such as 6 = 1 x 6 = 2 x 3 and 12 = 2 x 6 = 3 x 4 are counted once. That gives 18 different results.

questions.text: Three transparent glass pieces with different engravings are shown below. They are to be overlapped, one on top of the other, with the red corner exactly matching each other. What is the total number of triangles in the resultant figure?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Overlapped, the pieces form three nested squares (outer, middle, inner). The diagonal from top-right to bottom-left runs right across, and the other diagonal runs from the top-left corner only as far as the middle square's bottom-right corner. Triangles with their tip at the centre, standing on a side of one of the squares: 3 at the top, 3 at the left, 2 at the bottom and 2 at the right, so 10. Half-squares cut off by a diagonal: 4 in the inner square, 4 in the middle square and 2 in the outer square, so 10. Total 20.

questions.text: A diagram of three blocks A, B and C and their direction of movement is shown below. The blocks move continuously in units and change directions after hitting the side walls. From the given position, if block A moves at a speed of 2 units per second, and block B and block C move at a speed of 1 unit per second, what is the least time (in seconds) that is required for all blocks to align exactly one below the other?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The gap between the walls is 11 units and each block is 3 units long, so a block's left end moves between 0 and 8. A starts at 8 moving left, B at 3 moving right, C at 1 moving left. After 7 seconds: A has gone left 8 units in 4 s and then right 6, so it is at 6. B has gone right 5 to reach 8 and then back 2, so it is at 6. C has gone left 1 to reach 0 and then right 6, so it is at 6. No earlier time lines up all three, so the answer is 7.

questions.text: A UNION of two solids, a pentagonal prism and a hexagonal prism is shown below. The side view (on the right) depicts how the solids intersect. Visualise the new solid formed by their INTERSECTION (the part common to both of them). How many surfaces will the new solid have?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The side view looks along the pentagonal prism: the hexagonal prism shows two faces meeting at a middle edge, with flat faces at the left and right edges. The pentagon's left side lies on the hexagon's left face, and its right corner only touches the right face. So the common solid has 4 sloping hexagon faces (front and back), 1 left face shared by both prisms, and 4 pentagon faces (the pentagon's other sides). The right face only touches along a line. Total 9.

questions.text: A solid object made of cubes is shown below. This object is symmetric about all three axes, and does not contain cavities (no hollow spaces). How many cubes does the solid contain?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The solid has five layers. The top layer is a plus of 5 cubes. The next layer is a 3 by 3 square with one cube added at the middle of each side (13). The middle layer is a 5 by 5 square without its 4 corners (21). By symmetry the two layers below repeat 13 and 5. Total 5 + 13 + 21 + 13 + 5 = 57.

questions.text: A solid is drilled using a cylindrical drill in a direction, as shown below. How many surfaces will the solid have after the drilling is complete?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Start from the solid's faces before drilling, then follow the drill through it. A drilled hole adds its curved wall, and where the drill breaks through a face or crosses a slot, it can split one surface into two or join surfaces together, so look at each place the drill enters and leaves. Count each flat face and each separate curved wall once. IIT Bombay's final key gives 10 surfaces.

questions.text: The figure below shows a hinged structure made up of 12 sticks. The structure can be elongated and compressed by changing the angle ABR. As shown in the figure, the distance between B and Q is 150√6 (one hundred and fifty times root six) units when the angle ABR is 90 degrees. What will this distance be when the angle ABR is changed to 60 degrees?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: B to Q spans 5 rhombuses. The angle of each rhombus at B equals angle ABR, and its horizontal diagonal is 2s times the cosine of half that angle, where s is the side. At 90 degrees: \(5 \times 2s\cos 45^\circ = 5\sqrt{2}\,s = 150\sqrt{6}\), so \(s = 30\sqrt{3}\). At 60 degrees: \(10s\cos 30^\circ = 10 \times 30\sqrt{3} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 450\).

questions.text: In a new form of decimal system, the numbers 0 to 9 are represented by a new set of symbols. For example, the equation 1 + 4 = 5 is represented as equation (i). If in the solution to equation (iv) one digit appears twice, what number will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: From (i): the bar is 1, the arch with a right curl is 4, and the hook is 5. In (iii) a two-digit number minus one digit gives 14, so the number is in the twenties: the arch is 2, the box is 0, and the arch with a left curl is 20 - 14 = 6. In (ii), 4 + the double arch = the double arch with a curl, which leaves 3 and 7, so the double arch is 3 and the curled double arch is 7. In (iv) the first number is 313. The second ends in 6, and its first symbol is new, so 8 or 9: 313 + 86 = 399 and 313 + 96 = 409. Only 399 repeats a digit.

questions.text: What is the area (in cm2) of the black portion, if the square is of length 16 cm?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Split the 16 cm square into four 8 cm quarters (64 cm2 each). In the top-right and bottom-left quarters, the two white trapeziums each have parallel sides 6.5 cm and 1.5 cm and height 4 cm, so each is 16 cm2. That leaves 64 - 32 = 32 cm2 black in each of those quarters. The other two quarters each hold 16 cm2 of black. Total 32 + 32 + 16 + 16 = 96 cm2.

questions.text: The figure shows two concentric equilateral triangles with a circle within, such that the circle touches all the edges of the triangle. If the radius of the circle is √3 (square root of three), what is the total length of the star shaped outer border formed by the two intersecting triangles?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The circle is the incircle of each triangle. For an equilateral triangle, side = \(2\sqrt{3} \times\) inradius \(= 2\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 6\). The other triangle cuts each side into three equal parts of 2, and the star's border is made of 12 such parts: 12 x 2 = 24.

questions.text: Except for one number, all the four-digit numbers given below are written using a single font. Identify the number that does not use the same font as the other numbers.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Compare the same digit across all the numbers: the shape of each 1, 6, 7, 0 and 9, the thickness of its strokes, the shape of its curves and the ends of its strokes. Digits in one font look the same wherever they appear, so the number in a different font shows digits that differ from their copies in the other numbers. That number is 1190, the answer in IIT Bombay's final key.

questions.text: Two perspective views of the same solid object are shown below. Count the total number of surfaces in the object. Assume hidden surfaces to be flat.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Use both views to build up the object, then count its surfaces one at a time: the front and back faces, and every side wall around the outline. A new surface starts at each sharp edge, while a smoothly curving stretch counts as one surface. Assume the hidden surfaces are flat, as the question says. IIT Bombay's final key gives 22, and also accepts 23.

questions.text: The image given below is made out of separate pieces. What is the least number of pieces that need to be moved and/or rotated and/or flipped for achieving symmetry about the central vertical axis?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Compare each piece with its mirror partner across the dashed axis. The two ears differ, so one ear piece must change (1). The pupils of the two eyes point the same way instead of mirroring, so one pupil must be flipped (1). In the outer feather column on each side, the wider feather sits in a different row, so two feathers must swap (2). In each of the two inner feather columns, the notched and the pointed feathers are in swapped rows, so two pieces must swap in each (2 + 2). The right lower wing differs from the left (1). Total 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 9.

questions.text: A logo was designed by creating a pattern of orange petals using four semicircles. These petals were then inscribed in a green circular shape with an inner diameter of 14√2 (fourteen times square root of two) units, what is the area of the orange part in the logo? (Assume π = 22/7)
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The petals come from a square whose corners touch the green circle, with a semicircle drawn inward on each side. The square's diagonal is \(14\sqrt{2}\), so its side is 14 and each semicircle has radius 7. The four semicircles cover the square once and each petal twice, so petal area = 4 semicircles minus the square = \(2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 49 - 196 = 308 - 196 = 112\).

questions.text: Shyam runs a dairy. In his cattle herd, each white cow gives 12 litres of milk, each brown cow gives 7 litres of milk and each yellow cow gives 10 litres of milk every day. He has drawn a sketch of his herd which is shown below. Using this sketch, calculate the amount of milk (in litres) produced by his diary per day?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Count the animals by colour, using their heads, since the bodies overlap. Multiply each colour's count by that colour's milk per day (white 12, brown 7, yellow 10 litres) and add. IIT Bombay's final key gives 160 litres per day.
questions.defect: A count of the heads in the sketch gives 9 white, 6 brown and 7 yellow animals, which would make 9 x 12 + 6 x 7 + 7 x 10 = 220 litres. IIT Bombay's final key gives 160, which would follow if some of the animals drawn are not milking cows; the paper does not say how to tell them apart.

questions.text: Tile X was used to create a seamless pattern when arranged as shown below. Which tile(s) from the options will create a seamless pattern (pattern without gaps)?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: X is a square whose edges are reshaped so that the two edges at a corner are copies of each other turned 90 degrees about that corner. That is why four turned copies fit together around each corner in the pattern. C (corners on a 300-unit square, all four corners) and D (the curved version of X) follow the same rule, so they tile the same way. A has four dents but only two bumps, so its dents cannot all be filled. In B the matching edges point the same way, so neighbouring tiles cannot interlock.

questions.text: Which of the following statements related to Indian musicians is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Ustad Allah Rakha and Ustad Zakir Hussain are known for playing the Tabla

options.label: B
options.text: Pandit Nikhil Banerjee and Ustad Vilayat Khan are known for playing the Sitar

options.label: C
options.text: Ustad Ali Akbar Khan, Ustad Amjad Ali Khan and Dr. L. Subramaniam are known for playing the Violin

options.label: D
options.text: Pandit Ravi Shankar and Pt.Hariprasad Chaurasia are known for playing the Shehanai

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Ustad Allah Rakha and his son Ustad Zakir Hussain are tabla players, and Pandit Nikhil Banerjee and Ustad Vilayat Khan are sitar players, so A and B are true. In C, Ustad Ali Akbar Khan and Ustad Amjad Ali Khan play the sarod; only Dr. L. Subramaniam plays the violin. In D, Pandit Ravi Shankar played the sitar and Pt. Hariprasad Chaurasia plays the bansuri (flute), not the shehnai.

questions.text: Which of the options on the right can be formed by folding the profile shown on the left?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The net folds into a plus-shaped prism with a yellow plus and a green plus as its two ends, and 12 side walls. Fold the strips around the yellow plus. Going round it, starting at the left side of the top arm, the walls are blue, red, yellow, green, red, blue, red, green, red, yellow, red, green. Seen from the green end, the order runs the other way. B and C show yellow ends whose visible walls fit this sequence when the plus is turned by a quarter or half turn. D shows a green end that fits too. A has the same side walls as B but a green end, which would need the sequence in the opposite direction, so A cannot be folded.

questions.text: In a 3D structure made of cubes of equal size, an L shaped hole is made by removing a few cubes, as shown on the left. Which of the 3D structures in the options on the right would successfully pass through the L shaped hole, given that that they are also made of cubes of same size?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Look at each structure end on, along the direction it would travel: it passes if that outline fits inside the L-shaped hole. A, B and C have end-on outlines that fit the L, so they pass straight through. D does not fit straight through, but the wall is only one cube thick: D can go in part way, shift one square sideways while it is inside the hole, and then come out. So all four can pass, A, B, C and D.

questions.text:
The figure given below shows six bar charts corresponding to the volume of agricultural produce from farms of various farmers. The actual quantities are also shown in the figure. Red bars indicate tomatoes, green bars indicate leafy vegetables, and blue bars indicate berries. Assume that they have seen each other's bar charts. Who can correctly make at least one of the following statements?
(i) Everyone who produced any one item more than what I produced, she also produced every other item more.
(ii) Everyone who produced one item less than what I produced, she also produced at least one other item less.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Quantities (tomatoes, leafy, berries): Vinita 40, 60, 30; Nalli 40, 20, 60; Sukanya 40, 30, 30; Priya 70, 60, 20; Suneeta 20, 60, 20; Neela 60, 70, 60. Neela can say (ii): every other farmer who is below her in one item is below her in at least two (Priya, for example, is below in leafy and berries). Neela cannot say (i), because Priya beats her only in tomatoes. Vinita, Priya and Suneeta each fail both. For example, Nalli is below Vinita only in leafy vegetables and above her only in berries, Vinita is below Priya only in tomatoes and above her only in berries, and Vinita beats Suneeta in tomatoes but not in leafy vegetables.

questions.text: The figure shows four road networks. Which of these four road networks can be traversed by a traveller, such that the following challenge can be satisfied: “The traveller must cover all the roads in the network. She is allowed to visit a city more than once, but she is not allowed to travel on any road more than once. Also, the traveller must come back to the city where she starts.”
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Such a round trip exists only if every city has an even number of roads. In A, Delhi has 3 roads (Roorkee, Agra, Jaipur), and in C, Chennai has 3 (Bangalore, Selam, Trichi), so they fail. In B every city has 2 or 4 roads (Mumbai and Ratnagiri are joined by two roads), and in D Kolkata has 4 and every other city 2, so B and D can be traversed.

questions.text: The grid of squares shown in the figure is to be tiled (covered with tiles) with the tiles shown in the options. The covering tiles must not overlap and should not have gaps around them. Only four squares in the middle are not to be tiled. Once a tile is chosen, other tiles must be of that type only. Tiles can be flipped and rotated if required. Which of the tiles can be used to tile the given grid?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The grid is 10 by 10 squares without the 2 by 2 in the middle, 96 squares in all, split by the bold lines into four equal parts of 24 squares. Each tile must cover a whole number of squares in each part with no overlap and no gap. The L-shaped tile C covers every part. Tile D covers the parts only if its copies may be turned over, which the question does not settle, so IIT Bombay's final key accepts both C on its own and C with D. Tiles A and B leave squares that no copy can cover.

questions.text:
Suresh, Biju and Tina bring one gift each. When they meet, they swap their gifts in such a way that no one gets back what they had brought with them. The gifts are, a book, a pen, and a ball.
Suresh says: I gave my gift to the one who gave away the ball.
Biju says: I received my gift from the one who gave gift to the one who gave away the ball.
Tina says: I got what I always wanted.
Biju says: But Tina, you had to give away your pen.
Which of these statements is/are TRUE?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Tina brought the pen. With three people and no one keeping their own gift, the gifts go round in a circle. If Suresh gave to Tina, Tina would have given away the ball, but she gave the pen, so Suresh gave to Biju, Biju gave to Tina, and Tina gave to Suresh. Biju gave away the ball (Suresh's statement), so Suresh brought the book. So Biju gets the book, Tina gets the ball and Suresh gets the pen, which also fits Biju's statement.

questions.text: If the geometric solid blocks shown below, are cut along a single flat plane, which of these can have the cross section of a regular hexagon (all sides equal)? Assume, all blocks are extruded from polygons with sides of equal length.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A is a hexagonal prism: a cut parallel to its base gives a regular hexagon. B is a cube (a square extruded by its own side length): a slanted cut through the midpoints of six edges gives a regular hexagon. The pentagonal prism D has no pair of parallel side faces, so a hexagonal section cannot have its opposite sides parallel and equal, and any cut of the star prism C keeps star-shaped corners. So A and B.

questions.text: The following patterns are made on a wall by using ceramic tiles. Which of the given patterns is/are made from a single type of tile?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: A ceramic tile can be rotated on the wall but not flipped, so every spiral in a one-tile pattern must wind the same way. Follow each spiral from its centre outwards and note whether it turns left or right. In A and C all nine spirals turn the same way. In B the bottom-right spiral turns the other way, and in D the top-left spiral is a mirror image of its neighbours. So A and C.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about the areas of Indian states is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Arunachal Pradesh is larger than Kerala

options.label: D
options.text: West Bengal is larger than Uttarakhand

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Approximate areas: Arunachal Pradesh 83,700 sq km and Kerala 38,900 sq km, so A is true. Punjab is about 50,400 sq km, smaller than Assam at about 78,400 sq km, so B is false. Chhattisgarh is about 135,200 sq km against Jharkhand's 79,700 sq km, so C is true. West Bengal is about 88,800 sq km against Uttarakhand's 53,500 sq km, so D is true.

questions.text: Image P shows a portion of a larger photograph. Some operations have been done on that photograph using an image manipulation software. Image Q shows a portion of the resulting photograph. Identify the option(s) that specifies/specify the correct operations.

options.label: A
options.text: Rotate clockwise by 90 degrees, flip horizontally, then rotate clockwise by 90 degrees

options.label: B
options.text: Rotate clockwise by 180 degrees, then flip horizontally

options.label: C
options.text: Rotate clockwise by 180 degrees, then flip vertically

options.label: D
options.text: Rotate clockwise by 90 degrees, flip vertically, then rotate clockwise by 90 degrees

questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Comparing the grass patches, Q is P turned upside down as in a mirror, that is, a vertical flip. Rotating by 180 degrees and then flipping horizontally leaves a vertical flip, so B works. Rotating 90 degrees, flipping vertically and rotating 90 degrees again also leaves a single vertical flip, so D works. A and C both reduce to a horizontal flip, which does not match.

questions.text: Which of the following birds is/are native to (found in) India?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: A is a female Asian koel, with its spotted brown body and barred tail, common across India. B is a babbler, a common Indian bird. D is a drongo, with its forked tail, also found throughout India. C is a toco toucan, with its huge orange bill, which lives only in South America.

questions.text: The word given below uses a particular font. Which option(s) belongs/belong to the same font?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Compare each digit's shapes with the letters of 'Soulful': the contrast between thick and thin strokes, the round ball ends of strokes (as on the f), the shape of the curves and the serifs. A digit from the same font shares all of these. The 3 and the 5 do, so the answer is B and D, as in IIT Bombay's final key.

questions.text: A set of two frames with square openings when perfectly overlapped with each other allow light though it in certain patterns. Shown below are four sets of such frames. These frames are either hinged (A and B) or pivoted (C and D) to each other. Assuming that the red frames are fixed and the blue frames are allowed to move, which option(s) will allow light to pass through as in the pattern shown on the left?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Label the 4 by 4 holes by row and column. The target lets light through at row 1 column 3, row 2 column 2, row 3 column 3 and row 4 column 2. A hinged blue frame folds over as a mirror image across the hinge; a pivoted one turns 90 degrees about the corner pin onto the red frame. Light passes only where holes of both frames coincide. Doing this, A and C give exactly the target, while B and D give zigzags in the wrong columns.

questions.text: Refer to the tools below and read the statements. Based on what you can see, which of the following options is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: All tools have atleast one common working principle

options.label: B
options.text: All of them can be used for cutting fabric

options.label: C
options.text: Only one has spring back element, at least one has provision to crack nuts

options.label: D
options.text: Three of them have a provision to crack nuts

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The tools are circlip pliers, a nutcracker, a pair of scissors with looped handles and a betel nut cutter. All four are levers working about a pivot, so A is true. Only the scissors and the nut cutter can cut, and pliers or a nutcracker cannot cut fabric, so B is false. Only the circlip pliers carry a visible spring between the handles, and the nutcracker and nut cutter work on nuts, so C is true. Only two, not three, are made for nuts, so D is false.

questions.text: Multiple pages of a book are often printed on a single sheet. The sheet is later folded and cut appropriately to get the pages in a correct sequence and orientation. Mistakes happened while printing this particular 16 page booklet. The sheet was printed with pages numbered and oriented as shown on the left. The sheet was folded and cut in the sequence as shown on the right. Given this, which of the options is/are TRUE about the final booklet?

options.label: B
options.text: Page 11 is the last odd-numbered page

options.label: C
options.text: Page 4 is the first even-numbered page

options.label: D
options.text: All pages appear in the correct orientation

questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The notched corners show that each yellow page backs onto the next number (7 with 8, 10 with 9, 2 with 1 and so on). Fold the top half down over the front, then the right half over the left, then the left half over the right, and cut the top and right edges. Tracking each page through the folds, the booklet reads 5, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15, 16, 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, with every page upright. So 13 comes before 10, the last odd page is 11, the first even page is 6 (not 4), and all pages are correctly oriented.

questions.text: A bag contains 20 socks, of which 10 are white and 10 are black. If the socks are drawn without replacement, which of the options is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: If 1 sock is drawn at random, the chance that it is white is 50%

options.label: B
options.text: If 2 socks are drawn at random, the chance that both of them are the same colour is 50%

options.label: C
options.text: If 3 socks are drawn at random, the chance that at least two of them are the same colour is higher than if only 2 socks are drawn at random

options.label: D
options.text: If 4 socks are drawn at random, the chance that at least two of them will be the same colour is higher than if only 3 socks are drawn at random

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: A: 10 of 20 socks are white, so the chance is 50%. B: after the first sock, 9 of the remaining 19 match it, so the chance is 9/19, about 47%, not 50%. C: with 3 socks and only two colours, two must match, so the chance is 100%, higher than 9/19. D: with 4 socks the chance is also 100%, the same as with 3, not higher.

questions.text: In the figure below, a person is putting small packets of potatoes in one of the bins A, B or C. The packets are placed on a table, and the bins A, B and C are placed on tables which are lower in height as compared to table on which the packets rest. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Lifting the bag from the table and placing it in bin B will be less effortful compared to lifting and placing it in bin C

options.label: B
options.text: Lifting the bag from the table and placing it in bin A will be more effortful compared to sliding it in bin C

options.label: C
options.text: Lifting the bag from the table and placing it in bin B will be less effortful than sliding it to bin C

options.label: D
options.text: Sliding the bag from the table to bin C will be less effortful than lifting it and placing it in bin C

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Bin C sits right beside the packet table and lower than it, so a packet can simply be slid off the edge into it. Bins A and B are behind the worker, so using them means lifting and turning the body. Sliding into C is therefore the least effort, which makes B and D true. A and C claim that lifting into B is easier, which is false.

questions.text:
In a town, there are four kinds of persons: Mizrabs, Frets, Dictions and Scripts. People of any given kind play exactly two musical instruments. An instrument is played exactly by people of two kinds. Some Mizrabs play Tabla. Some Frets play Sitar. The kind that plays Harmonium does not play Sarod. The kind that plays Tabla does not play Sitar. Mizrabs and Dictions do not play the same instrument. Frets and Scripts do not play the same instrument. Dictions do not play Harmonium.

Which of the following is/are TRUE?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Four kinds play two instruments each and each instrument has two kinds, so there are four instruments: Tabla, Sitar, Harmonium and Sarod. Mizrabs and Dictions share nothing, so between them they play all four. Mizrabs play Tabla, so not Sitar, so their second is Harmonium or Sarod; if it were Sarod, Dictions would need Harmonium, which they do not play. So Mizrabs play Tabla and Harmonium, and Dictions play Sitar and Sarod. Frets play Sitar, so not Tabla, which leaves Tabla to Scripts (the second Tabla kind). All four statements hold.

questions.text: Which option replaces the question mark? (The paper prints only the picture for this question.)
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The figure pairs four Indian state names written in Sinhala script with their English names and asks for Maharashtra. Match the sounds: the ending of Gujarat in the script gives the syllable 'ra', and Kerala gives the 'r' sound. Option D starts with the 'ma' and 'ha' shapes, then the 'ra' syllable from Gujarat, and ends with 'shtra', so it reads Maharashtra. A, B and C read Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan and Tripura.

questions.text: The word given below uses a particular font. Which option belongs to the same font?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The word is set in a heavy, calligraphic Devanagari face with crisp, sharp edges, a headline whose left end is a pointed wedge cut diagonally underneath, and angular counters. Option A repeats that pointed, diagonally cut headline and the clean sharp curves. B and C have rough, wobbly outlines, and D has a blunter headline end and a squarer counter.

questions.text: Which option will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The background is a repeating pattern of overlapping ovals, so the missing square must continue the ovals exactly where they are cut off at the four edges of the gap. Following the ovals across the top, bottom and side edges, only B lines up with all of them. A is the same pattern shifted sideways, while C and D are different parts of the pattern.

questions.text: An envelope made of a single piece of paper is taken, and a few cuts are made on it. The envelope and the cuts are shown below. Identify the resulting figure when the envelope is unfolded?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The envelope is a square sheet whose four corners are folded to the centre, so unfolded it is a larger square turned 45 degrees with the flap tips at its corners. Each triangle cut goes through a flap and the back, giving two triangles: one in place and one mirrored across the folded edge. Each notch on an edge is cut through a fold, so it opens into a whole shape: a V notch becomes a square and a straight notch becomes a diamond after the 45 degree turn. This gives a 4 by 4 grid: triangle, square, square, triangle on top; diamond, triangle, triangle, diamond; diamond, triangle, triangle, square; triangle, square, diamond, triangle. Only B has this layout with every triangle pointing the right way.

questions.text: Shown in the four figures A, B, C, and D on the right, are broken lines drawn on a transparent sheet. Each figure is folded over along the dotted lines as shown. Identify the correct option that will generate the motif shown on the left.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Folding each side flap over its dotted line mirrors its lines onto the middle square, and the flap's outer edge lands on the vertical centre line. The motif needs both diagonals, the two curved arcs on each side of each diagonal, and the two centre lines, each unbroken. Only in A do the flap pieces exactly fill the gaps left in the middle panel; in B, C and D some arc or diagonal is left with a gap.

questions.text: A light source is attached to a rod fixed in the centre of the ceiling of a square room. This source rotates 360 degrees with the rod as its axis. This source projects a red beam of light onto the four walls of the room. This setup is shown in the isometric view and the side view in the figure below. Identify the correct path of the beam of light on the four walls of the room.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The beam points downward at a fixed angle, so the farther it travels before hitting a wall, the lower it lands. The middle of each wall is closest to the light, so the spot is highest there, and the corners are farthest, so it is lowest there. The beam sweeps a cone, and a cone cut by a flat wall gives a smooth curve, so each wall shows a smooth arch that is highest in the middle and dips at the corners, as in A.

questions.text: The figure below shows the top view, the front view, and the side view of a three- dimensional solid object. What is the minimum number of surfaces that a solid with these views, can have? Assume that there are no hidden lines.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Take a cube and trim it with a sphere centred at the cube's centre that passes through the midpoints of the cube's edges. Each of the 6 faces is left as a flat circle touching the four sides of the face, which gives the square with the circle inside in every view, with no hidden lines. The curved sphere surface remains only at the 8 corners, and these pieces touch each other only at points, so they are 8 separate surfaces. That is 6 + 8 = 14 surfaces.

questions.text: Sheetal is running. Which option denotes the most natural pose?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: A natural running stride has the body leaning slightly forward over the front leg, the front foot off the ground, and bent arms swinging opposite to the legs. In C the torso leans forward and the front foot is lifted. In A the upper body is held upright and back, B looks like a lunge with the front foot planted, and in D the arms hang straight down instead of swinging.

questions.text: Identify the correct profile of the cricketer that corresponds to the given front pose.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Read the front pose limb by limb: which hand holds the bat and where it points, which leg is crossed in front, and which foot rests on its toes. A side view keeps all of these, only seen from the side, so the nearer limbs hide parts of the farther ones and the crossed leg and the raised heel still show. Check each profile against every detail of the front pose. Only C keeps them all.

questions.text: Seema on the left, is looking at a mirror. Which option shows her reflection correctly?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A mirror swaps left and right, so every detail must move to the opposite side together: the hair bun, the finger touching the pimple, the earring and the direction of the eyes. In C the bun, the finger and the pimple all move to the left side and the eyes look the mirrored way. A keeps the bun on the same side, while B and D move the bun but leave the face or hand unflipped.

questions.text: Kavita is holding a lit torch below her face as she narrates a ghost story to her friends in a dark room. Which option shows the lighting correctly?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: A torch held below the face lights the surfaces that face downward: the neck under the chin, the lower cheeks, the underside of the nose and the area just below the eyes, while the top of the head stays dark. B shows exactly this. A is lit from above (bright hair), C from one side, and D lights the brows and hair edge as if from above.

questions.text: Which option correctly represents the top view for the given perspective view?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The object is two upright plates crossing at right angles, seen from a corner: the tall grey plate runs away to the right and the shorter pink plate runs away to the left. Because the grey plate is taller, its top edge runs unbroken across the crossing in the top view, which rules out B. Allowing for perspective, the pink plate's near end (on the right) is much closer to the crossing than its far end, about one third of its length. Turning the top view so that the grey plate is vertical with its near end at the bottom puts the pink plate's near end on the right, so the crossing sits about a third of the way in from the right, as in D. A crosses the pink plate at its middle, and C is the mirror image of D.

questions.text:
A milkman is returning from his trip on his bicycle. He has two empty containers of 5 litres and 3 litres hanging on one side of the bicycle, and a full 8 litres milk container on the other side. He was not able to ride the bicycle properly. So he stopped and decided to distribute the milk, so that the load becomes balanced on the both sides of the bicycle. Unfortunately he has forgotten his measuring cup on his last stop.

How many minimum turns will it take for him to be able to distribute the milk into two equal halves to balance the load? Ignore the weight and other material properties of the containers and the bicycle.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Write the contents as (8 L can, 5 L can, 3 L can), starting at (8, 0, 0). Pour 8 into 5: (3, 5, 0). Pour 5 into 3: (3, 2, 3). Pour 3 into 8: (6, 2, 0). Pour 5 into 3: (6, 0, 2). Pour 8 into 5: (1, 5, 2). Pour 5 into 3: (1, 4, 3). Pour 3 into 8: (4, 4, 0). That is 7 pours, and checking every possible sequence shows no shorter way leaves 4 litres on each side.

questions.text:
Four students P, Q, R and S are shown a box which contains a few white balls, and a few red balls. Their teacher asks each of them individually to make a statement. The teacher knows that exactly one of them is a liar and others are not. From the statements that they make, the teacher is able to find out who the liar is. Given below are the statements made by the students. Who is the liar?

P says: There are equal number of red balls and white balls.
Q says: P is a liar and there are 3 red balls and 2 white balls.
R says: Q is not a liar and there are some red balls and some white balls in the box.
S says: R is not a liar.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: If S lied, R would be a liar too: two liars. If R lied, S's statement 'R is not a liar' would be false: two liars. If Q lied, R's statement 'Q is not a liar' would be false: two liars. So the only possibility is P. Then Q is truthful (3 red and 2 white, not equal), R and S are truthful, and everything is consistent.

questions.text: Shown below is an image with straight lines, in which, a tilted-square has been cut out. From the given options identify the missing cut out of the square that completes the original image.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The cut-out is a square turned 45 degrees, so each option must be turned back by 45 degrees. Mark where each line meets the cut-out's edges: the thick line enters about two thirds of the way up the upper-left edge and leaves at the matching point on the lower-right edge, exactly opposite, and three thin lines meet the edges at fixed points. Turning A by 45 degrees puts the thick line and all six thin-line ends exactly on those points. In B, C and D the two ends of the thick line are not exactly opposite each other, so they cannot fit.

questions.text: A T-shirt with folding marks and the folding sequence is shown on the left. The folding is done backwards and perfectly along the lines. After completing all the folds, the T-shirt is then turned around. Identify the correct folded T-shirt from the options on the right.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Folds 1 and 2 tuck the two sides behind the middle panel. Fold 3 folds the lower half backwards and up, so the front of the lower middle panel now faces the back, upside down, with the dark hem at the top. Turning the shirt around shows this panel turned through 180 degrees: hem on top and the zigzags reversed both left to right and top to bottom. C matches. A and D are only flipped top to bottom, and B is shifted sideways.

questions.text: A paper strip is rolled and then punched by a triangular punch, as shown below. After unrolling the paper strip, what would be the pattern of holes on the paper?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The punch passes straight through the middle of the roll, so it cuts every turn of the strip twice, once on each side of the centre. The front view shows the punch slanting, entering higher on one side and leaving lower on the other, so the holes on the two sides of each turn sit at different heights. Unrolled, the holes therefore alternate high and low, and the gap between them grows as the turns get larger towards the outside. Only option D shows alternating high and low holes with widening gaps.

questions.text: Identify the option that will replace the question mark.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The same solid turns a little further in each frame: it tips over and also turns clockwise in the picture plane, so its long side gets flatter from frame to frame and the small cube on its face shows fewer faces. The next frame should continue both turns: the long side at a slightly lower slant than in frame 4 and the small cube still showing two faces split by a vertical edge, as in frame 4. Option C fits this best.

questions.text: How should the two solids be joined in order to form a tetrahedron?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Fig 1 is a tetrahedron abcd and Fig 2 is a pyramid with apex i on the four-sided base fghe. The two must be glued along matching triangular faces with matching edge lengths. Face abc matches face fgi: the short edge ab fits the short edge fg, and the long edges ac and bc fit fi and gi. So a goes to f, b to g and c to i, and the faces around d then line up with the pyramid's faces to make one larger tetrahedron. Option A pairs g with e, which are not on one face, and options C and D pair edges of different lengths.

questions.text: Perspective view of an object is shown below. The object is rotated 180 degrees around y-axis (when viewed from a point on the positive y-axis towards the origin) and then similarly rotated 180 degrees around z-axis. Which of the following perspective view options will be the result of the rotations? Assume positive x and y axes point in the direction of the viewer.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A half turn about the y-axis followed by a half turn about the z-axis is the same as one half turn about the x-axis: x stays, while y and z both reverse. So every bar along x keeps its direction, and every bar along y or z flips. Trace the rotated rod from the hooked end: up a short way, along minus x, down a long way, along plus x, along plus y, along minus x, a short step along plus y, up a long way, and along plus x to the square end. Option A follows exactly this path; B, C and D do not.

questions.text: On a glass entrance door of a building, there is an arrow sign pointing towards the newly shifted office space on the first floor. The sign is printed on a paper and pasted on the outside of the door using two tapes, one at the top-middle, and other at the bottom-middle. Due to the frequent use of the door, the top tape is peeled off, and the paper falls with the bottom tape holding it. After falling, from inside the building one can see the arrow sign pointing towards the Southwest direction. If that is the case, in which direction was the arrow sign originally pointing to (as seen from outside)?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: When the top tape comes off, the paper swings down about its bottom edge, so the picture turns upside down and the printed side now faces the glass. Turning it upside down flips up and down; looking at it from the other side of the glass flips left and right. Both flips together are a half turn, so the arrow now points the opposite way. An arrow seen pointing Southwest (down and left) was therefore pointing Northeast (up and right).

questions.text: A cube and a truncated cone are shown below. The cube has dimensions 10 × 10 × 10 units. The truncated cone has a base diameter of 12 units, height of 11 units and top diameter of 6 units. Imagine these two solids are intersecting while positioned coaxially on the same base. Further imagine the cube vanishes completely along with the intersected portion of the truncated cone. What remains?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The cone's radius falls from 6 at the base to 3 at the top, so at height h it is \(6 - 3h/11\). The cube reaches 5 units from the axis at the middle of each face, so the cone pokes out of each face only where the radius is more than 5, that is below \(h = 11/3\), about 3.7 units. That leaves four small separate curved pieces at the bottom, one outside each face. Above the cube (height 10 to 11) a thin slice of the cone, only 1 unit thick, is also left. Option A shows four small pieces and a thin top slice.

questions.text: Afreen is a teacher. She decides to give biscuits to her students Javed, Jai, Joshua and Jaspreet. She has biscuits of four different sizes, all of which have the same perimeter and thickness. The proportions of the biscuits are shown below. She asks Javed, Jai, Joshua and Jaspreet, in that order, to pick biscuits in descending (largest to smallest) order of volume. Which biscuits should Jai and Jaspreet pick up respectively?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: With equal thickness, volume follows area. For rectangles with the same perimeter, the area is largest for the square and shrinks as the rectangle gets longer and thinner. So the order is P (square), Q, R, S (thinnest). Javed takes P, Jai takes Q, Joshua takes R and Jaspreet takes S.

questions.text: A crocodile at point P sees four meatballs at A, B, C and D across the river. The crocodile moves with the same speed on ground as well as in water. If the speed of river is half the speed of crocodile, which meatball can it catch in the shortest time?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: P is directly above C, and the crocodile must cover 100 m of land, 200 m of river and 100 m of land across the flow. The fastest any crossing can be is when it heads straight across all the way, taking 400 m divided by its speed. While swimming straight across the 200 m, the river (at half its speed) carries it 100 m to the left. It lands 100 m left of the line through C, which is exactly the meatball B, so B is reached in this least possible time.

questions.text: Which number will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Each diamond holds two numbers, their sum and their difference. First diamond: 24 and 11 give 35 and 13. Second: 32 and 15 give 47 and 17. Third: 40 and 19 give 59 and 21. Fifth: 56 and 29 give 85 and 27. The four places turn one step clockwise from diamond to diamond. In the fourth, 48 and the missing number add to 72 and differ by 24, so the missing number is 24.

questions.text: Which black shape from the options will match the white shape in the figure, using simple rotation.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Going round the white shape clockwise from the circle you meet the sharp triangle point, a step out to the rectangle, the small spike on the long edge close to the rectangle's corner, and a small step back to the circle. Turning the white shape about three quarters of a turn brings it exactly onto C. Option B is the same shape flipped over, which a rotation cannot produce, and A and D do not fit the white outline.

questions.text: The figure below shows a 3 × 3 cube with 4 colours. The same coloured shapes are detached and shown separately for reference. Identify the shape of the red block from the given options.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Green is a C of 7 cubes filling the left layer, yellow is 4 cubes (a column of three with one arm) at the front, and grey is a C of 5 cubes on the right. That accounts for 16 of the 27 cubes, so red has 11. They form a plus sign of 5 cubes in the second layer from the front, with a block 2 wide and 3 tall behind its centre and right columns. Option B shows exactly a plus sign in front of a 2 by 3 block; D has an extra front cube at the bottom right.

questions.text: Which option will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The green and orange circles and the yellow circle at the left of row 2 never move. The other yellow circle and the two cyan circles sit on the ring of six circles around the second circle of row 3, and each moves one place round that ring per frame. Moving them one more step puts yellow at the third circle of row 2, one cyan at the third circle of row 3 and the other cyan at the second circle of row 4. That is option B; D also moves an orange circle, which never moves.

questions.text:
Jaya, Sushama, Rama, Dilip, Sudhir and Arun are doctors working in a hospital specialising in gynaecology, neurosurgery, paediatrics, orthopaedics, anaesthesia and intensive care, not necessarily in that order. What is Rama’s specialisation if the following conditions are to be met:
- Jaya, Arun and Sushama work together.
- Neurosurgeons always need the help of orthopaedic surgeons in the operation theatre.
- Orthopaedic surgeries cannot happen on the same days that gynaecological surgeries happen.
- Gynaecologists need paediatricians on standby during their operating hours.
- Though Sudhir and Dilip work together, neither has ever met Sushma in the hospital.
- All specialisations except intensive care need to work with Arun, the anaesthetist.
- Doctors don’t work together other than as mentioned above.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Arun is the anaesthetist. The working teams are neurosurgeon with orthopaedic surgeon, and gynaecologist with paediatrician, each with Arun; the intensive care doctor works with nobody. Jaya and Sushama work together with Arun, so they are one of these pairs, and Sudhir and Dilip, who never meet Sushama, are the other pair. The only doctor left is Rama, who must be the intensive care specialist.

questions.text: Shown below on the left is a Ferris wheel which is not in motion. A photographer has clicked a photograph of the Ferris wheel while it was rotating at its maximum speed in an anti-clockwise direction. Which of the options below is the image that he has captured?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Each cabin hangs from a pivot on the rim and is free to swing. When the wheel turns at its top speed, the motion makes every cabin swing away from hanging straight down, so in a photograph taken then the cabins are tilted, in a pattern that depends on where each one is on the wheel. Compare how the options tilt the cabins all the way round. The photograph that shows the cabins as they hang on the turning wheel is D.

questions.text: Which option will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Work across each row and see how the lines in the squares change from one square to the next: which lines stay, which are added, and where the vertical line moves. The same change happens in every row, so apply the change in the last row to the square before the question mark. The square that results is D.

questions.text: Identify the correct order of rotation.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Figure 9 shows the nine pairs of lines on an upright square grid. In the other figures the same grid is turned: in 6, 3, 2 and 1 it is turned clockwise by growing amounts, and in 8, 7, 4 and 5 it is turned anticlockwise by growing amounts, in steps of roughly 15 degrees. Putting the figures in order of angle gives 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 8, 7, 4, 5, which is the path drawn in option B.

questions.text: The following images are iconic art forms/products of certain countries. Identify the correct set of countries they all can be predominantly attributed to. The individual countries in each set are in a random sequence.
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The four objects are a whirling dervish figure (Turkey), a beckoning cat or maneki-neko (Japan), a pair of painted wooden couple dolls (India) and nested matryoshka dolls (Russia). Option C names exactly these four countries. The other options bring in Mongolia, Burma, Afghanistan or Pakistan, none of which matches any of the objects.

questions.text: Refer the following images of a metal artefact made using traditional manual tools, skills and processes. Identify the correct set of operations required to make it.
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The deer is Bastar-style wrought iron work: strips of iron are heated and hammered into shape (forging), bent to form the legs and neck, punched to make the row of dots on the body, and twisted to make the spiral horns. No molten metal is poured, so casting (options B and D) is not used, and the dots are punched marks, not drilled holes (option C).

questions.text: Refer to the chairs shown below. Which of the following options is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: P is most stable in terms of centre of gravity and R is made of least number of visible parts

options.label: B
options.text: S is made of least number of visible parts and Q is most stable in terms of centre of gravity

options.label: C
options.text: P is most stable in terms of centre of gravity and S is made of least number of visible parts

options.label: D
options.text: R is ergonomically comfortable and Q is most stable in terms of centre of gravity

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Check each claim against the pictures. P stands on four legs at the corners of a broad square frame, braced by rails, with its seat inside the base, so its centre of gravity stays well within its support: it is the most stable. Q has only three legs under a triangular seat that overhangs them, so it is less stable. S is made of two curved boards and a round seat, the fewest visible parts, while R has many parts including metal fittings. So the true statement is C.

questions.text:
Refer to the following image of a wooden product and read the statements below.
1. It has provision for cracking nuts, and it has a good grip
2. It has a good grip, and it has provision for opening cans as well as cracking nuts
3. It has provision for a grinding nuts, and its making involves drilling, twisting, and casting
4. Its making involves drilling, turning, and twisting
Which of the following options is correct?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The object is a wooden screw nutcracker: a nut placed in the cup is crushed by turning the threaded knob, and the knob's rounded, ridged shape gives a good grip, so statement 1 is true. It has nothing for opening cans, so statement 2 is false. It does not grind nuts and wood is never cast, so statement 3 is false. Option D calls statement 1 false, so it cannot be right; option A is correct.

questions.text: Shown is a quadrant that is mirrored first on x-axis and then on y-axis. Identify the correct complete figure from the given options.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Mirroring the quadrant on both axes makes a circle that is symmetric left to right and top to bottom. In the quadrant, the two bars nearest the vertical axis are not joined away from the centre, so the full figure has no H shape at the top and bottom centre; this rules out A and B. The crossbar between the third and fourth bars sits about a third of the radius from the horizontal axis, and only D has it at that height on both sides; in C the left-hand crossbars are closer to the middle than the right-hand ones, so C is not symmetric.

questions.text: Thamarai’s father has made a roti for her lunch. She folds the roti in the following sequence and packs it into her lunch box. Identify the folded roti.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Fold 1 brings the top half down over the front along the horizontal line, so the back of the top half now faces up. Fold 2 then folds the right part back along the vertical line, leaving the left part on top. The face we see is the back of the roti's top-left quarter, turned upside down by the first fold. That part of the back has a cluster of small spots and one larger spot near its lower edge, and turning it over gives exactly the spot pattern of option B. The large burnt spots of the front's lower-left quarter would show if neither fold covered it, and no option shows them.

questions.text: An unwrapped cube is shown below. This cube has cuts of specific shapes on all sides. When the cube is folded, what would be the view as seen from direction X?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: In the net, the four faces in the row wrap round the cube, so the first and third are opposite, and the second (downward triangle) is opposite the fourth (upward triangle). The folded cube shows the small hexagon on top, the large hexagon on the left and the upward triangle on the right, which is the face seen from X. Because the shapes are cut out, you look through the upward triangle and see the opposite face's downward triangle behind it. Its three edges cut off the three corners of the upward triangle, which is option D.

questions.text: The four figures below show a hand gripping a cylinder. In which of these figures, will the grip exert the maximum force?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: A hand is strongest in a power grip, where the fingers wrap fully round the object and meet the thumb. In D the cylinder is just the right size for the fingers and thumb to close round it and touch. In A and C the cylinder is too wide for the fingers to wrap round, so they push with weaker, stretched fingers, and B is only a fingertip pinch on a thin rod.

questions.text: Four cut-outs of shapes (labelled p, q, r, s) are shown below. Using one or more of the cut-out pieces, how many unique combinations can be made that will create a square/rectangle?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: p and r are equal right-angled isosceles triangles with legs equal to the side of the square q, and s is a parallelogram slanted at 45 degrees with the same height. The sets of pieces that make a square or rectangle are: q alone; p and r (a square); p, q and r (a 2 by 1 rectangle); p, r and s (the triangles fill the slanted ends of s to make a 2 by 1 rectangle); and all four pieces (a 3 by 1 rectangle). No other set works, so there are 5 combinations.

questions.text: The figures show simplified shapes of the neck portion of the vertebral column of a horse. Which of the options is most correct?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: A horse's neck bones do not follow the top line of the neck. They form an S-shaped curve: low down near the chest at the base of the neck, then rising steeply to join the skull at the poll, just behind the ears. Option B shows this S-curve ending at the top of the head. A and C run as a gentle straight slope, and D joins the head too low.

questions.text: How many times is the area of the outermost triangle compared to the area of the innermost triangle?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The figure alternates equilateral triangles and circles: each circle is the incircle of the triangle outside it, and the next triangle is drawn inside that circle. An equilateral triangle's inscribed circle has half the radius of its circumscribed circle, so each new triangle has half the side of the one before and a quarter of its area. Two such steps give \(4 \times 4 = 16\).

questions.text: Which option will replace the question mark as the frog jumps in an animation sequence?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The frames show the frog sitting, pushing off with legs stretched, flying level at the top of the jump, and finally sitting again. The missing frame is the way down: the body tips nose-down, the front legs reach forward to land and the back legs are still stretched out behind. Option C shows this. A looks like a take-off, B has the back legs bent upward, and D shows the frog hanging upright.

questions.text: Which option will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.subtopic: Matching a part to the whole
questions.solution: The two pieces fit together into one hexagon made of rings, each ring split into six segments. Put each coloured segment of both pieces in its place. Outer ring: tan, navy, tan, green, tan, navy going clockwise from the top left. Second ring: grey-green top left and top right, red on the right and bottom left, navy bottom right, green on the left. Third ring: red, green, navy, red, grey-green, navy. Centre triangles: grey-green, navy, red, navy, green, red. Only A matches every segment: B has red and green swapped in the second ring, C has green at the bottom left of the third ring, and D swaps two centre triangles.
